tagline.text: Exploring a seven-level limestone cave in Tanay

location.label: Location
location.text: Calinawan Road, Barangay Tandang Kutyo, Tanay, Rizal

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (flooding and mud in the rainy season)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (half a day for the deeper levels)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–800 (per person, covering admission, a shared guide and tricycle)

children.text: Calinawan Cave is a multilevel limestone cave in Barangay Tandang Kutyo, Tanay, Rizal. With a guide you can explore levels 1–2 in a little over an hour, and it pairs well with Daranak Falls for a half-day trip.

Calinawan Cave is a natural cave in Barangay Tandang Kutyo, Tanay, Rizal, east of Manila. It is described as a large cave system of many levels, chambers and openings, and local information says it has seven levels in all. Most visitors see only the easy levels 1–2, while levels 3–5 are an exploration route that involves crawling through narrow gaps, so experienced people go in with a guide and set aside half a day. Levels 6–7 are said to be closed. The cave entrance is inside privately owned land, so the landowner's caretaker collects the entrance fee. Calinawan Road is described as the first paved road on the right when heading from Daranak Falls Road toward the falls, and the road to the entrance is unpaved, so cars must drive slowly.

Several stories are told about the cave. A local guide says it was first discovered in 1901 by a guide's grandfather, and that refugees hid here during the Philippine–American War and Japanese soldiers used it during World War II. The name is said to come either from "linaw," meaning "to clear," or from "nakalinawan," meaning "to reconcile," and some accounts add that during the revolt against Spain, Filipino revolutionaries and American troops settled their disputes inside the cave. These are lore without confirmed evidence, so enjoy the guide's explanations as stories.

The inside of the cave is mostly dry and many stalactites and stalagmites have stopped growing, but there are stretches with large columns and sparkling crystals that catch visitors' eyes. Some chambers drip water from above, and low ceilings and narrow passages follow one another. Below level 2 you can see virtually nothing without light. The cave is also known as a filming location for the TV dramas Encantadia and Ang Probinsyano. On the other hand, it has been pointed out that painting and glitter applied to the level 1 walls during one drama's filming caused damage, and local conservation discussions continue. The cave has not been completely mapped, so there may be side passages even the guides do not know, and some openings are said to lead to a cliff. For that reason, never leave the set route and go in alone.

This guide is for travelers who have already seen places such as Daranak Falls and Masungi in Tanay, and for beginners new to caving. Many of the entrance and guide fees quoted come from 2015–2018 blogs, so it is safest to check with the Tanay tourism office before you go. In the rainy season the cave floods and may close or become muddy, so plan your trip for the dry season. The inside of the cave is cool and humid and sweat does not dry easily, so a light jacket is useful, and keep your phone in a waterproof pouch. If your group is larger than five, you need two tricycles, so calculate transport costs for your group size in advance and you will not be left scrambling on site.
You cannot enter without a guide, and levels 1–2 need no special skills, so beginners can do them. The tour is reported to take about
30 minutes to 1 hour

, and helmets and flashlights can be borrowed. Many reviews say the flashlights are weak, so bring your own headlamp. The paths are dark but wide enough to walk through, and no special skills are reported to be needed. A guide tip is optional, but many visitors give about
per hour as a guideline.

Level 2 has a large rock column called the "eerie column" and stalactites. Dripping and dry sections are mixed, and crystals sparkle when you shine a light. Some places have low ceilings, so watch your head.

You have to squeeze through narrow gaps and your clothes will get dirty. It takes half a day and the guide may ask for an extra tip. It is recommended only for experienced people or those used to caving. A guide may also lead you to less-known parts of the cave, but this is not done in the rainy season, so plan your trip for the dry season.

blocks.title: Cave lore and the origin of the name

children.text: The guide tells stories of the discovery, hideouts in wartime and the origin of the name. Some passages are said to lead to Montalban, Baras and Pililla, but this is unconfirmed. That the stories behind the name branch in several directions itself shows that this cave has long been remembered by villagers, so do not miss the enjoyment of listening to the commentary.

blocks.title: The cave as a filming location

children.text: TV productions such as Encantadia are known to have been filmed here. There has been controversy over damage by film crews, so as a courtesy visitors should not touch the walls or write graffiti.

A small store near the cave entrance sells sandwiches, soft drinks, halo-halo, mais con yelo and biscuits. It is good for a quick rest after the cave. The store is small, so think of it as a snack stop rather than lunch.
Daranak Falls is reported to be about
15 minutes
from the cave by car. See the
Daranak Falls
guide for the falls, and since the falls usually close at 5 PM, it is better to go to the cave first.

The long travel makes the schedule slip easily. Confirm the falls' closing time with your guide or local residents. The last van may stop running early, so it is safer to reach the terminal before 5 PM.

Take Manila East Road through Taytay, Angono, Binangonan, Cardona, Morong and Baras into Tanay.

Signs are scarce, so search for the cave by name on Waze or Google Maps and confirm with locals.
The dry season (November–May) is best. In the rainy season the cave floods and becomes muddy, and entry is restricted in heavy rain.
In the hot months the cool inside of the cave becomes a refuge from the heat. Do not explore the deeper levels in the rainy season.
The inside of the cave is cooler than outside, but the humidity is high and the floor is wet, so sweat does not dry easily and a change of clothes helps.
The quietest time is a weekday morning, and on weekends the road to Calinawan Road can be crowded because of vehicles heading to Daranak Falls. If heavy rain is forecast, postpone your trip.

A small store near the cave sells snacks such as sandwiches, soft drinks and halo-halo. For a proper meal, it is better to eat in Tanay town or at restaurants around Daranak Falls. Bring plenty of water and your own snacks. The store in front of the cave also sells mais con yelo and biscuits besides sandwiches and soft drinks, but the toilet and wash facilities are basic, so bring your own change of clothes.

There are small hotels and resorts in Tanay town, and several places to stay near Daranak Falls. You can also return to nearby Antipolo and stay there. If you come out late in the afternoon, you can also have dinner in Tanay town before heading back.
Bring your own headlamp and spare batteries. Many reviews say the flashlights provided are weak.
Wear clothes you do not mind getting dirty and shoes that do not slip.
A camera or a phone with a night mode that handles low light will give better photos.
Ask your guide about the route and safety rules first, and follow their instructions.
Some reviews say you can swim for free in a small lagoon near the cave, so ask your guide.
A towel, a change of clothes and a plastic bag are handy.
Daranak Falls usually closes its gate at 5 PM, so keep that in mind when planning.
Whether children are allowed and whether guides work on Sundays are not stated in the published sources, so ask the Tanay tourism office (0998-988-1590) beforehand.
This is private land, so pay the entrance fee at the entrance and follow the rules.
Having cash in small denominations makes it easier to pay the entrance fee and the guide's tip.
In the rainy season it is dangerous because of flooding and mud, and levels 3–5 go through narrow gaps, so do not enter without an experienced person and a guide.
Below level 2 you cannot see without light, so always carry a light.
Some stretches have low ceilings and narrow passages, so be careful not to hurt your head and knees.
Do not touch the walls, write graffiti or break stalactites. Damage has been reported.
Do not enter the closed sections (levels 6–7).
Fees and guide group sizes differ between sources, so confirm them locally.
It has been pointed out that some stretches were damaged during film and drama shoots, and conservation discussions are under way. Access may change, so check before you visit.
